title: Dates and the datetime index
summary: Real dates instead of strings, partial-date indexing and the .dt accessor.

steps.title: Dates are not strings
body: A CSV gives you dates as text. Text looks fine until you compute with it:
`pd.to_datetime` turns text into real points in time (`Timestamp`, or a `datetime64` column), which sort
chronologically, subtract into durations, and know their weekday:
Converting the date column is nearly always the first thing you do with time-stamped data.

steps.prompt: Your `orders` table has a `date` column of strings like `"2024-07-14"`. Why convert it with `pd.to_datetime` before analysing it?
options: So it sorts by time, subtracts into durations, and supports weekday, month and resampling operations
Because pandas refuses to store dates as strings
It makes the file smaller on disk
Strings cannot be used as a DataFrame column
steps.explain: Strings are stored happily, they just don't behave like time. Only real datetimes know that 2024-9-30 comes before 2024-10-02.
Subtracting two timestamps gives a `Timedelta`; `.days` is its whole number of days. February 2024 has 29 days.

steps.title: A DatetimeIndex
body: Put the dates in the **index** and the rows become a time series. Two things become easy:
s.loc["2024-01-31":"2024-02-02"]    # a date range, both ends included
**Partial-string indexing** picks a whole year (`"2024"`), month (`"2024-02"`) or day by its text.
Sort the index first: slicing needs the dates in order.

steps.explain: `"2024-02"` matches 2 Feb and 15 Feb (7 + 10). A date slice includes both ends. After sorting, the first date is 30 January.

steps.prompt: Turn the `when` column into a sorted time index, then count the rows in May 2024.

steps.title: The .dt accessor and durations
body: A datetime **column** has a `.dt` accessor with the parts of each date; a **DatetimeIndex** has them directly:
Durations are `Timedelta`s. For calendar steps ("one month later") use `DateOffset`, which knows months differ in length:
t + pd.DateOffset(months=1)     # same day next month (31 Jan -> 29 Feb)

steps.prompt: `ts = pd.Timestamp("2024-07-04 15:30")`. Match each expression to its value.
steps.explain: `normalize()` drops the time of day, which is handy for grouping by date.

steps.title: Days between
prompt: Write `days_between(start, end)` that takes two date strings like `"2024-02-01"` and returns the number of whole days from
`start` to `end` as an `int` (negative if `end` is earlier).
template: Dojo.eq("end before start is negative", -10, days_between("2024-05-11", "2024-05-01"))
Dojo.check("returns an int", isinstance(days_between("2024-01-01", "2024-01-02"), int), "return the .days of the difference")

steps.title: Sales by weekday
prompt: Write `weekday_totals(df)`. `df` has a `date` column of **strings** and an `amount` column. Return a dict from weekday name
(`"Monday"`, ...) to the total `amount` on that weekday. Only weekdays that appear need to be in the dict.
hints: You can group by a Series: `df.groupby(names)["amount"].sum().to_dict()`.
template: Dojo.eq("the caller's date column is untouched", "2024-06-01", dojo_df2["date"].iloc[0])

steps.title: A time-indexed table
prompt: - `by_date(df)`: `df` has a `date` column of strings plus other columns. Return a **new** DataFrame indexed by the converted
dates, sorted oldest first (the `date` column becomes the index).
- `month_total(df, month)`: `df` is what `by_date` returns; `month` is text like `"2024-02"`. Return the total of the
`amount` column in that month as an `int`.
hints: `out = df.copy()` first, so the caller keeps their strings.
template: Dojo.check("the index is a DatetimeIndex", isinstance(dojo_t.index, pd.DatetimeIndex), "convert with pd.to_datetime and set_index")
Dojo.eq("the original still has its date column", "2024-02-10", dojo_raw["date"].iloc[0])
